sections.title: 3 From Discrete to Continuous: A Continuous Relaxation Perspective
sections.text: 3 From Discrete to Continuous: A Continuous Relaxation Perspective Continuous Relaxation. Let [LaTeX: \mathcal{V}=\{1,\dots,V\}] 𝒱 = { 1 , … , V } \mathcal{V}=\{1,\dots,V\} denote the vocabulary of size [LaTeX: V] V V . We define the discrete token space as the set of one-hot vectors [LaTeX: \mathcal{X}=\{\delta_{1},\dots,\delta_{V}\}\subset\{0,1\}^{V}] 𝒳 = { δ 1 , … , δ V } ⊂ { 0 , 1 } V \mathcal{X}=\{\delta_{1},\dots,\delta_{V}\}\subset\{0,1\}^{V} . Associated with the vocabulary is an embedding matrix [LaTeX: \mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times D}] 𝐔 ∈ ℝ V × D \mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times D} . The embedding function maps a token index [LaTeX: i] i i to a continuous vector [LaTeX: \mathbf{e}=\mathbf{U}_{i}] 𝐞 = 𝐔 i \mathbf{e}=\mathbf{U}_{i} . We denote the continuous embedding space as the convex hull of the token embeddings: [LaTeX: \mathcal{E}=\text{Conv}(\mathbf{U})\subset\mathbb{R}^{D}] ℰ = Conv ​ ( 𝐔 ) ⊂ ℝ D \mathcal{E}=\text{Conv}(\mathbf{U})\subset\mathbb{R}^{D} . A soft token is any vector [LaTeX: \tilde{\mathbf{e}}\in\mathcal{E}] 𝐞 ~ ∈ ℰ \tilde{\mathbf{e}}\in\mathcal{E} that can be expressed as [LaTeX: \tilde{\mathbf{e}}=\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{p}] 𝐞 ~ = 𝐔 ⊤ ​ 𝐩 \tilde{\mathbf{e}}=\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{p} , where [LaTeX: \mathbf{p}\in\Delta^{V-1}] 𝐩 ∈ Δ V − 1 \mathbf{p}\in\Delta^{V-1} lies on the probability simplex. This formulation relaxes the categorical selection into a continuous domain. Iterative Refinement in Continuous Domain. Unlike standard MDLMs which predict [LaTeX: p_{\theta}(X^{0}\mid X^{T})] p θ ​ ( X 0 ∣ X T ) p_{\theta}(X^{0}\mid X^{T}) iteratively over the discrete vocabulary, our method models the reverse process as an iterative refinement loop in the continuous domain [LaTeX: \mathcal{E}] ℰ \mathcal{E} . Specifically, let [LaTeX: X^{T}] X T X^{T} denote the masked input sequence and [LaTeX: \mathbf{E}^{T}] 𝐄 T \mathbf{E}^{T} be its corresponding embeddings, where each element of [LaTeX: \mathbf{E}^{T}] 𝐄 T \mathbf{E}^{T} belongs to [LaTeX: \mathcal{E}] ℰ \mathcal{E} . We introduce auxiliary token states [LaTeX: \mathbf{Z}^{T}] 𝐙 T \mathbf{Z}^{T} to enable continuous token evolution. The refinement process is governed by a transition function [LaTeX: \Phi] Φ \Phi , which recursively updates both the continuous embeddings and the token states: [LaTeX: (\mathbf{E}^{t-1},\mathbf{Z}^{t-1})=\Phi(\mathbf{E}^{\geq t},\mathbf{Z}^{\geq t})] ( 𝐄 t − 1 , 𝐙 t − 1 ) = Φ ⁡ ( 𝐄 ≥ t , 𝐙 ≥ t ) (\mathbf{E}^{t-1},\mathbf{Z}^{t-1})=\Phi(\mathbf{E}^{\geq t},\mathbf{Z}^{\geq t}) . Through successive applications of [LaTeX: \Phi] Φ \Phi , the model progressively purifies the noisy input until it reaches the terminal [LaTeX: \mathbf{E}^{0},\mathbf{Z}^{0}] 𝐄 0 , 𝐙 0 \mathbf{E}^{0},\mathbf{Z}^{0} . Finally, [LaTeX: \mathbf{E}^{0}] 𝐄 0 \mathbf{E}^{0} is mapped back to the discrete domain to produce the output sequence [LaTeX: X^{0}] X 0 X^{0} .

5 Experiments
sections.text: 5 Experiments 5.1 Experimental Setup We employ LLaDA-Instruct-8B ( Nie et al., 2025 ) as our primary backbone for fine-tuning. To evaluate cross-model consistency, we also apply our method to LLaDA-1.5 ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , Dream-Instruct-7B ( Ye et al., 2025 ) and D2F-LLaDA ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , the last of which serves as the base model for our blockwise diffusion experiments. For fine-tuning, we utilize the S1K dataset ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ) and train the pretrained model for a default duration of 10k steps using continuous trajectory supervision. Evaluations are performed across several mathematical and reasoning benchmarks, including Countdown ( Pan et al., 2025 ) , GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , MATH500 ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) , and SVAMP ( Patel et al., 2021 ) . Table 1 compares EvoToken-DLM against the original LLaDA-Instruct-8B and the FT-baseline across multiple reasoning benchmarks. EvoToken-DLM predominantly surpasses both baselines, exhibiting substantial performance leaps under varying configurations. Specifically, at [LaTeX: \frac{NFE}{Gen\ Len}=1] N ​ F ​ E G ​ e ​ n ​ L ​ e ​ n = 1 \frac{NFE}{Gen\ Len}=1 , our method yields average accuracy gains of [LaTeX: 17.45\%] 17.45 % 17.45\% on Countdown, [LaTeX: 3.08\%] 3.08 % 3.08\% on GSM8K, [LaTeX: 2.06\%] 2.06 % 2.06\% on MATH500, and [LaTeX: 3.23\%] 3.23 % 3.23\% on SVAMP compared to the original model. These results underscore the superiority of our soft token evolution framework in enhancing reasoning capabilities and generation quality. Additional results with different block sizes are presented in Appendix E.3 , and qualitative comparisons are presented in Appendix E.5 . Importance of Intermediate States. Figure 5 illustrates the ablation study on the presence of intermediate refinement states. The performance drop observed when removing these states confirms that the gradual transition from mask to soft-token is essential for the model to iteratively refine its predictions. Qualitative Visualization. We provide a qualitative visualization of the inference process in Figure 6 . By tracing the evolution of a selected subsequence, we observe how initial uncertain tokens progressively converge into precise and coherent results. This visualization confirms that EvoToken-DLM effectively implements a progressive refinement mechanism, allowing the model to iteratively calibrate its predictions within the diffusion framework. Additional qualitative visualization results of the inference process are presented in Appendix E.4 . Compatibility with KV-Caching. To further demonstrate the practical efficiency of EvoToken-DLM, we integrate it with the KV-caching mechanism as proposed in Fast-dLLM ( Wu et al., 2025b ) . This integration is essential to ensure that our adaptive token evolution does not interfere with the accelerated inference pipelines of DLMs. As reported in Table 2 , we evaluate the performance of EvoToken-DLM equipped with KV-caching against the baseline on Countdown. The results indicate that our method consistently maintains superior performance with KV-caching across various computational budgets, proving its seamless integration with the KV-caching mechanism. Robustness across Thresholds. We further adopt another parallel generation strategy using the confidence threshold proposed in Fast-dLLM ( Wu et al., 2025b ) to replace the fixed NFE setting. This allows for a more flexible allocation of computational resources during inference. We analyze the sensitivity of our method to different thresholds on the MATH500 dataset, with KV-caching enabled. As illustrated in Figure 7 , EvoToken consistently outperforms the binary masking baseline given the same average token budget per step. These results demonstrate the superior adaptability of EvoToken-DLM. Table 2: Performance comparison on Countdown with KV-caching. EvoToken integrates seamlessly with KV-caching mechanism. We evaluate the transferability of our approach by applying continuous trajectory supervision to the Dream-Instruct-7B pretrained base. As shown in Figure 8 , the improvements observed in the primary model consistently generalize to the alternative backbone. This consistency underscores that EvoToken-DLM serves as a general enhancement for diffusion language models. Additional results based on LLaDA-1.5 are presented in Appendix E.1 . Extension to Blockwise Diffusion. To further validate the versatility of EvoToken, we extend our method to the blockwise diffusion framework, specifically using D2F-LLaDA as the base model. As illustrated in Figure 9 , EvoToken significantly outperforms the binary masking baseline, proving its robustness and adaptability. Inference Efficiency. Figure 10 illustrates that EvoToken-DLM introduces only negligible latency compared to standard MDLMs, with the marginal overhead stemming primarily from the element-wise addition of token embeddings during the refinement process. Such minimal overhead, alongside substantial improvements, makes EvoToken-DLM highly practical for real-world deployment. Impact of Top- [LaTeX: K] K K Filtering. In Figure 11 , we analyze the sensitivity of the model to different top- [LaTeX: K] K K settings during the refinement process. EvoToken-DLM shows robust performance across a wide range of [LaTeX: K] K K values, consistently outperforming the baseline. An additional ablation study on the mixing ratio [LaTeX: \alpha] α \alpha is presented in Appendix E.2 . More analyses regarding rapid adaptation from pretrained MDLMs are presented in Appendix D .

sections.title: Limitations
sections.text: Limitations While our approach enables rapid adaptation from pretrained MDLMs to EvoToken-DLM via lightweight supervised fine-tuning, it faces training challenges when applied to models initialized with autoregressive (AR) priors. The inherent discrepancy between unidirectional AR pretraining and our iterative bidirectional refinement process leads to increased training difficulty and slower convergence for AR-based backbones. We provide a detailed comparative analysis in Appendix D .

sections.title: Appendix C More Implementation Details
sections.text: Appendix C More Implementation Details C.1 Detailed Descriptions of Training Dataset and Evaluation Benchmarks We utilize a combination of high-quality instruction-tuning data and diverse mathematical benchmarks. Training Dataset. • S1K ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ) : A high-quality dataset featuring 1,000 diverse and challenging problems, each accompanied by distilled reasoning traces and solutions to facilitate complex chain-of-thought reasoning. Evaluation Benchmarks. We evaluate the performance of our model across the following four benchmarks, covering a spectrum of arithmetic and logical difficulty. • Countdown ( Pan et al., 2025 ) : A combinatorial arithmetic task that requires models to reach a target value using a specific set of numbers and basic operators. • GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) : A collection of 8.5K grade-school math problems requiring 2–8 steps of multi-step arithmetic reasoning. • MATH500 ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) : A subset of 500 challenging high-school competition-level problems selected from the MATH dataset. • SVAMP ( Patel et al., 2021 ) : A benchmark of 1K elementary math word problems designed to test model robustness against linguistic variations in narratives. C.2 Training Configurations for Continuous Trajectory Supervision To fine-tune the model under the progressive token evolution mechanism, we employ the following training configurations. The model is trained on the S1K dataset ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ) for a total of 10k steps. • LoRA Configuration: The LoRA adapter is applied to the query, key, and value projections. We set the rank [LaTeX: r=128] r = 128 r=128 , LoRA alpha [LaTeX: \alpha=256] α = 256 \alpha=256 , and a dropout rate of [LaTeX: 0.05] 0.05 0.05 , with no bias parameters tuned. • Optimization Settings: We use a learning rate of [LaTeX: 1e-5] 1 ​ e − 5 1e-5 with a total batch size of [LaTeX: 8] 8 8 . • Sequence Handling: The maximum sequence length is truncated at [LaTeX: 1,024] 1,024 1,024 tokens. • Continuous Simulation: Following our proposed framework, the number of continuous simulation steps [LaTeX: \Delta\tau] Δ ​ τ \Delta\tau is set to [LaTeX: 4] 4 4 . For blockwise processing, the current block size is fixed at [LaTeX: 512] 512 512 . During training, the number of transition tokens [LaTeX: |S|] | S | |S| is dynamically sampled from the set [LaTeX: \{1,2,4,8\}] { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } \{1,2,4,8\} to enhance the model’s robustness across varying generation densities. The mixing ratio is stochastically sampled from a uniform distribution [LaTeX: \mathcal{U}(0.5,1.0)] 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0.5 , 1.0 ) \mathcal{U}(0.5,1.0) . C.3 Inference and Evaluation Setup To ensure a fair and reproducible evaluation, we standardize our inference parameters across all datasets. We employ a decoding temperature of [LaTeX: 0.5] 0.5 0.5 and fix the random seed to [LaTeX: 42] 42 42 to eliminate stochastic variance. For the proposed refinement mechanism, we perform a grid search for the hyperparameter [LaTeX: \alpha] α \alpha within the candidate set [LaTeX: \{0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9\}] { 0.5 , 0.6 , 0.7 , 0.8 , 0.9 } \{0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9\} and report the performance associated with the optimal [LaTeX: \alpha] α \alpha for each setting. For evaluations based on Dream-Instruct-7B ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , we set the default generation length to 256 with [LaTeX: 128] 128 128 NFEs. For evaluations based on D2F-LLaDA ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , we set the default maximum generation length to 512.
